title: I Went to Banff To Say Yes To Everything
text:
I Went to Banff To Say Yes To Everything
If you’re looking for a reason to switch on your out-of-office reply, we’ve got you covered. Wellbeing-driven, wanderlust-focused, our travel series takes you to places worth the trip, not only to escape the grind, but to spark some joy, reset, recover, and return ready for whatever’s next. Let us show you the world.

I arrived in Canada with a smile. I had packed exactly the right amount of underwear, my clothes were coordinated, and I had definitely remembered toothpaste. As a chaotic Type B traveler, this was growth, and the right start to what was supposed to be a relaxing trip in the mountains. 

I’d been invited by Moxy Banff and Marriott Bonvoy Moments for three days of exploring the Canadian Rockies, from Lake Louise and Moraine Lake to the Bow River. 

But I had also arrived carrying something I hadn’t packed: the lingering feeling that I should always be doing more. 

My life revolves around work, deadlines, and an endless stream of notifications, and I had gotten very good at being productive and increasingly bad at being present. Even on vacation, part of me was usually thinking about what needed to happen next. 

Somewhere along the hour-long drive to Moxy Banff, surrounded by mountains and increasingly spotty cell service, I decided whatever was waiting for me back home could wait. 

It was time to fully go out of office. 

My Wishes for This Trip 

As I settled into my flight and gazed out the window in the kind of dreamlike state only a Pisces could understand, I took a deep breath and set two intentions for the trip. 

Number one: Become more present. I wanted to enjoy the little moments. The bees landing on flowers, the textures, and the moments I would one day wish I could get back. To push me to do so, I brought my camera. Photography used to be one of the main ways I made sense of the world before it became something I was always too busy to do. On this trip, my camera would become my North Star. 

Number two: Do some scary sh*t. Before the trip even started, I knew kayaking was on the itinerary. Through Marriott Bonvoy Moments, the entire experience had already been planned for us, from where we’d go to the people we’d get to experience it with. It was the kind of access that made trying something completely outside of my comfort zone feel a little more possible. 

And as a proud mammal who can’t even swim, voluntarily paddling down the Bow River felt slightly unhinged. Better yet, unnatural. 

To raise the stakes, Marriott invited two-time Olympian Evy Leibfarth to join us. Yes, the Evy Leibfarth, the first American woman to medal in Olympic canoe slalom after taking bronze in the women’s C1 event at the 2024 Paris Games. 

So, yes, the stakes felt pretty high. Still, I wanted to do it. The goal wasn’t to suddenly become fearless; it was to stop allowing fear to keep me from truly living. I would leave Banff with at least one new skill and that was enough. 

What I Packed 

For once in my life, I actually packed according to the itinerary. With only three days in Banff, I kept things simple and leaned heavily on Oner Active’s Lori Harvey Day-to-Night Capsule: the SoftMotion Racerback Dress for hiking, plus the Soft Motion Straight Leg Pants and matching High Waisted Leggings for everything in between.  

I also packed for the important business of smelling good. During the day, I wore Blank Body Sculpt Body Oil in Sweet Plantain, a warm, plantain scent that felt surprisingly fitting for the mountains. I also paired it with Vaseline’s Sunlit Glow Body Shimmer Gel Oil for extra hydration. At night, I switched to my Phlur Island Swim body mist. 

However, if I could go back and repack, I’d grab a heavier coat. Sure, the daytime was warm, but at night, my little airport hoodie was not going to cut it. And Banff is the kind of place you want to walk around and take in, so don’t let being a little chilly cut your night short. 

Day 1 

Banff, for the record, is not a real place. 

It’s the kind of town you’d imagine being dropped off somewhere along the Polar Express route. The entire town is framed by mountains, so no matter which direction you look, there’s this absurdly beautiful backdrop behind everything. 

Our home for the weekend, Moxy Banff, somehow fit right into all of it. The hotel had this retro, mid-century mountain-lodge feel that made it playful without letting you forget you were surrounded by the Canadian Rockies. After checking in, we dropped our things and walked into town, which took around 20 minutes. As a former New Yorker, this qualified as basically next door. 

That evening, I found myself at Pizzeria Sophia, eating the best lemon pasta of my life. I struck up a conversation with my server, who was from Australia. He was working at the restaurant while training to become a snowboard instructor. 

Over the next three days, I would meet person after person who had come to Banff for the same reason: there was something here they loved enough to rearrange their lives around. They were people who had moved their entire lives across the world to chase something I would personally categorize as some “scary shit”! Without even realizing it, my wish to do some scary shit was already manifesting, with every person I met showing me what was possible when you stopped letting fear make your decisions. 

Day 2 

Some places are so beautiful your brain has a hard time computing that what you’re looking at is real. Lake Louise was one of them. The water was this almost ridiculous shade of blue, surrounded by mountains so massive that the whole thing looked less like a real place and more like one of those default MacBook screensavers. 

At Moraine Lake, I climbed to a viewpoint overlooking mountains that had existed long before me and would continue existing long after me. Everything felt enormous, and all the little things that normally consumed my attention suddenly felt small. 

I instinctively reached for my phone to take a photo and realized I didn’t have service. 

There were no emails to answer, feeds to refresh, or notifications competing for my attention. Whatever was happening beyond those mountains would have to wait. For the first time in a while, I felt my shoulders loosen and my breath steady. All I had in front of me was the landscape and my camera. 

I photographed the water, the mountains, and the people who appeared impossibly tiny against them. I started noticing composition and light again. I began looking at the world the way I used to, when taking photographs was something I did simply because it made me happy. 

Then I looked down at one of my first images and low-key? 

I still had it. 

Day 3 

If day two was about slowing down, day three was about learning how to say yes, even after I had already said no. 

We set out that morning to kayak the Bow River alongside Evy Leibfarth. I was excited, despite having done absolutely zero research into what kayaking actually entailed. I climbed into a tandem kayak with another girl and almost immediately realized that I had no idea what I was doing. We could not get in sync. Within minutes, we were both frustrated, barely moving, and I was ready to call it, so I got out. 

I had already decided I was good. I could walk, take some pictures, and enjoy the scenery from the very safe comfort of land. But everyone around me kept encouraging me, and eventually they convinced me to try again, this time in my own kayak. 

Once I stopped worrying about throwing someone else off, I found my rhythm. I paddled down the river, surrounded by mountains, passing a beaver dam along the way. I realized the thing I had been terrified to do was actually…peaceful. 

Even our kayaking instructor had moved from England to Banff because he wanted to snowboard. Another person who had crossed an ocean because there was something here he loved enough to follow. 

After kayaking, we met back up with Evy for a multi-course lunch at The Maple Leaf Steak & Seafood. It was the perfect ending for what was supposed to be a terrifying day. Later that afternoon, I wandered through Banff by myself, stopped in museums, took pictures, and followed whatever looked interesting. There was no schedule to check and nowhere I needed to rush off to next. That afternoon, I got to simply exist. 

What to Know Before You Go 

I went in August, which was the right call. The weather was warm enough to spend my days outside, the mountains were still snow-dusted in the distance, and I could hike without having to become a winter-sports person overnight.

You can’t drive a personal car to Moraine Lake. Parks Canada closed Moraine Lake Road to personal vehicles in 2023, so you’ll need to arrange transportation ahead of time. There are several approved shuttle and public transit options available, but reservations can fill up quickly.

Yes, you need a park pass. Banff is inside Banff National Park, which means visitors need a valid Parks Canada park pass. You can purchase one ahead of time or when you arrive, but I’d handle it before the trip so there’s one less thing to think about once you’re there.

Moxy Banff is walkable to downtown. One of my favorite parts of staying at Moxy was being able to walk into town instead of constantly worrying about a car. Downtown Banff is roughly a 20-minute walk from the hotel, so pack comfortable shoes.

Check Marriott Bonvoy Moments before your trip. The kayaking experience I did was available through Marriott Bonvoy Moments, where Marriott Bonvoy members can use points to bid on or redeem experiences that go beyond a traditional hotel stay—from food and music to sports and outdoor adventures.

Bring good walking shoes, some layers, and an itinerary… or don’t. You’ll find something to do either way.

What I Wish I’d Known 

Sometimes, when you’re in this mindset of wanting to heal, it’s easy to start experiencing your life in the third person. I found myself mentally checking in: Am I doing enough? Am I fulfilling the wishes I set for myself? Is this changing me yet? At some point, even healing can become another thing to accomplish. I wish I’d known that being present is actually much simpler than that. Sometimes, it’s just losing service on a hike and not panicking about it. Letting the email wait. Letting yourself look around without needing to document, respond to, or make meaning out of every second. 

Eventually, I would have to go home, open my laptop, and return to real life. The emails, deadlines, and responsibilities weren’t going anywhere. 

Banff was enough. 

About the Writer 

Jessika Hardy is a freelance writer and social strategist at Refinery29 Unbothered, covering travel, culture, and all things internet. When she’s not online, she’s probably baking banana bread or flipping through records. 

Editor’s note: This trip was hosted by Moxy Banff and Marriott Bonvoy Moments. All opinions and experiences are the writer’s own.

title: I Went to Sensei Lānaʻi to Find My Baseline
text:
I Went to Sensei Lānaʻi to Find My Baseline
If you’re looking for a reason to switch on your out-of-office reply, we’ve got you covered. Wellbeing-driven, wanderlust-focused, our travel series takes you to places worth the trip, not only to escape the grind, but to spark some joy, reset, recover, and return ready for whatever’s next. Let us show you the world. 

I’ve been to Hawaiʻi many times and visited other islands, but Lānaʻi is the one people talk about with deep lore. I’d always wanted to see it for myself, and I’d been obsessing about Sensei Lānaʻi, A Four Seasons Resort. It’s a wellness retreat in the upcountry of the island, and the seclusion and specificity were exactly what I wanted. So I reached out about planning a trip, and worked with their wellbeing team to build an itinerary that met me exactly where I was: exhausted, but full and inspired. It also made room for my fiancée, who was in a similar place in their work life.

I was six months into a new job as SVP of Brand & Content at R29Unbothered, and those months had been a satisfying whirlwind, full of new skills and the strange relief of finally being inside an industry I’ve loved from the outside for years. They had also been six months without a single day off, and it was showing up in small, unglamorous ways. I’d been carrying the same book from room to room for weeks, reading the same page four nights in a row and retaining none of it. I’m also dealing with some ongoing health stuff, chronic pain that has quietly reorganized my life. I needed to find my baseline, or at least remember I had one — and I had a feeling Sensei could help.

My wish for this trip was specific:  I wanted to surrender to nature, stay off my phone, finish the book, and come home knowing more about my body than I knew when I left. I was excited to find out. So my fiancée and I made our way to Lānaʻi.

What I Packed

• A few vintage silk and linen pieces that I could transition in and out of.
• EltaMD UV Daily Hydration+ SPF 50. I don’t leave the house without it, let alone the state.
• Augustinus Bader The Ultimate Soothing Cream. The single thing that has done the most for my literally soothing my dermatitis.
• Marie Veronique Balancing HypoTonic and Barrier Restore Serum. These two products have changed my skin and hold up in any climate.
• My Clyde Swim Bucket hat In Black. Basic enough to live in all day, which is what the property asks of you.
• The Bond-Eye Sofie Triangle and Serenity Brief, both in black
• My HealthyLine TAJ-Mat, the twenty-by-twenty travel size. It’s the heaviest thing in my bag but I have to have it when I travel, just in case I have a pain flare up
• A Terrible Strength: The Hidden Crisis of the Black Womb and Your Survival Guide to Healing by Dr. Kemi Doll. I hadn’t been able to put it down, so I needed to take it with me.

The Days

Day 1
We landed and were fed before anyone asked anything of us. There’s a Nobu on the property, and dinner that first night was the prime tenderloin tobanyaki, with caramelized onions, shiitake and asparagus, all of it deglazed in sake and yuzu soy and still moving in its hot ceramic dish when it reached the table. Nobody handed me an intake form. Nobody asked me about my goals. We ate, and then we walked back through the gardens into the quietest dark I’d been in for a long time. There were critters everywhere, frogs and lizards moving through the leaves, and the whole property had this nighttime ambient noise running underneath it. It helped us both drop in.

Day 2

The next morning I walked out of my room and did what became my daily practice for the rest of the trip, which was to slow all the way down and take in the flora and fauna on the property.

Tropical flowers in bloom everywhere. The colors you move through on that walk do their own kind of healing work before you ever get to the spa or sit down for a wellbeing session.

Then I had what became my breakfast ritual meal the whole trip, this delicious Japanese breakfast with perfectly brined salmon. 

Then I sat down for a private wellbeing session that paired breathwork with biometrics, which meant they clipped a little node to my earlobe and tracked my heart rate variability while I breathed, so I could watch my own nervous system move in real time. I’ve been meditating since I was seventeen. I had never had proof. The practitioner watched the numbers come in and told me that I drop into a parasympathetic state easily, faster, she said, than most people she works with. That was comforting to hear as a longtime meditator. I had never seen the quantitative impact my practice has on my physiology, and I loved finding out. We spent the rest of the day at the pool, doing nothing, on purpose.

Day 3

The next day we rode horses through the wilderness of Lānaʻi. The stables were beautiful, saddles and tack oiled and knolled like a still life, everything set exactly in its place. My horse was named Spirit and he was exceptionally gentle with me. I loved taking in the energy of the island with equine support, and hearing its history from the ranch hand leading the ride. 

Then we had Lomi Lomi massages, side by side. Lomi Lomi is an indigenous Hawaiian massage practice, rhythmic and deeply connective. The closest analog I’ve found is Thai massage. Both are built on momentum rather than stillness. There is rocking, there is stretching, there is very little lying flat and receiving. You move with the practitioner. This is also the practice that made me a person who gets massages at all: in college in South Africa, the bodyworker I saw was a Pacific Islander who specialized in it. Being returned to it two decades later, in the place it came from, allowed me to be reflective about my own journey, and left me in reverence of Hawaiian culture and their unique somatic intelligence.

Day 4
On day four I went clay shooting, which I had never done in my life and turned out to be pretty good at, which was a surprise. Here’s what I didn’t know: shooting is a full body, hyper focused experience. While you’re tracking a target there is simply no room in your head for anything else, and it’s an immediate off switch.
Later that afternoon I tested my VO2 max. If you haven’t come across it, VO2 max is the measure of how much oxygen your body can actually take in and put to use when you’re working hard. It’s the cleanest proxy we have for cardiovascular fitness, and it happens to be one of the better predictors we have of how long and how well you get to live. The test itself was simple. I walked on a treadmill for about eight minutes breathing into an oxygen device, starting off very slow. Because of my chronic pain, they put me on an incline instead of having me run. The chronic pain has cost me cardiovascular fitness, and seeing that arrive on a screen was less painful than I had braced for. The trainer was matter-of-fact about it, which was exactly what I needed. Honestly, I think this was one of the key pieces that helped inform my baseline. Even though I look strong and feel strong, my cardiovascular capacity is really affected right now. Learning my VO2 max helped me understand that there is still so much room for me to get back to a better baseline.

Day 5
I saved Watsu for the last day, because it’s one of my favorite somatic practices. At Sensei Lānaʻi they call it aquatic bodywork. It’s shiatsu performed in water, with weights on your legs so that you float rather than hover, and I am deeply in love with it. It always feels like a return to the most primordial support there is. We did ours in one of the spa hale, the thousand-square-foot structures tucked into the gardens with their own pools. It turned out to be the right way to say goodbye to the property, release the trip, and get myself ready to go home. A beautiful ritual to close on.

What to Know

Before you go

• The remoteness is the whole proposition. You get there on a thirty-minute semi-private flight from Honolulu on Lānaʻi Air, which is included in the stay, and once you’re on Lānaʻi, you’re on Lānaʻi. If you want to be out and about, this isn’t your trip. 
• The property is eighteen and over, which is a good part of why it stays as quiet as it does. 
• Sensei sits up at Kōʻele in the upcountry, while beach access is down at Hulopoʻe Bay at the sister Four Seasons, about thirty minutes away on a shuttle that runs hourly. The two properties feel like different climates, so pack for both.

Wish I’d known

The wellbeing programming is more rigorous than the setting lets on. The grounds are lush enough that you could mistake this for an escapist trip, and then your VO2 max arrives on a screen. If you go the fitness optimization route, be prepared to blend a serene, nutritive environment with hard information about your body: your cardiovascular capacity, your biometrics, how you actually meditate. For some people that’s too much of a juxtaposition. For me it was exactly what I needed. And if you want something even more restorative and less data driven, they have a rest and sleep focused program.
Oh, and my book. I finished the last few pages on the flight home.

About the Writer
Erica Chidi is SVP of Brand & Content at R29Unbothered 

Sensei Lāna’i hosted a portion of this stay. All opinions are the author’s own.

title: If You’re A Pants-And-A-Top Girl, This One Fall Piece Changes The Whole Look
text:
If You’re A Pants-And-A-Top Girl, This One Fall Piece Changes The Whole Look

Right now, the one fall trend that fashionistas are keeping on hand for the cooler fall temperatures is the all mighty suede jacket. It’s rare to come across a jacket that feels luxuriously cool and everyday-wear appropriate. Which is why, when you do, you hold on to that versatile wardrobe hero like a prized trophy.

The sumptuous texture was all over the streets during New York Fashion Week, and it’s easy to see why. Suede has a richness that adds instant depth to practically any outfit without making it feel overly styled.

Imagine throwing one over your go-to jeans-and-a-T-shirt combo or bring a modern edge to your workwear trousers. The finishing touch instantly elevates an otherwise casual look without giving off any I’m-trying-too-hard vibes. On the other side of the outfit spectrum, picture pairing one with a lace-trimmed slip dress. It works just as seamlessly, adding a cool finishing touch without distracting from the rest of the look. That’s the beauty of a great suede jacket: It doesn’t shout for attention, no matter how you style it.

There’s a leather collar-trimmed design by Aligne at the top of my wishlist. The zip-up jacket has that made-to-never-go-out-of-style wow factor that helps justify the price over time. Siempre makes one with the silhouette of a blazer and a belted finish. It’ll look incredibly chic with Bermuda shorts and your go-to boots or flared denim and flats. Want something that can carry you from fall into winter? Avec Les Filles has a longline option with a collar that can be flipped up for a true street-style-star finish.

I could wax poetic about the closet-worthy suede jackets popping up in stores right now for days, but I’ll spare you and get to the good stuff. Keep reading for Refinery29’s curation of the latest and greatest suede jackets— plus, plenty of inspiration for how to style them this fall.

title: These Rainy-Day Chic Outfits Were The Hero Of New York Fashion Week
text:
These Rainy-Day Chic Outfits Were The Hero Of New York Fashion Week

There’s nothing worst then the torment of a rainy day ruining your plans. One thing I’ve learned from this season of New York Fashion Week is to never let a few drops of water stop you from serving up a photo-worthy look. Fellow show goers seem to be on the same page, too. A few simple styling tricks combined with functional accessories can make dressing to impress a cinch, even during a flood watch.

I like to coordinate my umbrella with my outfit. It, after all, becomes part of the look if you’re carrying it around. If you’re doing a bit of walking, which is kind of a non-negotiable in NYC, the right footwear matters. Ahead, you’ll see a combination of cute, timeless rain boots mixed with glamorous yet surprisingly practical shoes that can handle a wet sidewalk without sacrificing the entire outfit.

But the biggest takeaway from NYFW street style? Dressing for bad weather doesn’t mean every single thing you wear needs to be waterproof. Instead, it’s about choosing where to be practical. A rain boot can make a frilly lace dress work in a downpour. A hood can eliminate the need for an umbrella altogether. And sometimes a closed-toe shoe, cropped hem pants, and a really good parasol are enough to get the job done.

Ahead, I’m breaking down five rainy-day outfits worth stealing from the streets of New York Fashion Week — including my own.

DashDividers_1_500x100

This might be my favorite rainy-day styling equation because the contrast is so good. Instead of letting practical green rain boots dictate the rest of the outfit, they’re paired with a delicate white lace dress and cropped trench cape.

It works because nothing is pretending to be something it isn’t. The boots are unapologetically functional. The dress is unapologetically pretty. And the trench bridges the two, giving the look enough structure that the combination feels intentional rather than like someone changed shoes at the last minute.

It’s also the easiest formula here to recreate: Take the outfit you actually wanted to wear, then swap your precious footwear for a great rain boot.

The styling trick: Don’t build your entire outfit around your rain boots. Sometimes the coolest way to wear them is with something completely unexpected.

DashDividers_1_500x100

If there was ever an argument for making the hood part of the outfit, this is it.

Instead of treating rain protection as something to throw on at the last minute, this look builds it directly into the styling. The black hood creates a dramatic frame around the face while allowing those vivid green trousers to remain the focal point. Even better, their cropped, slightly flared silhouette avoids the cardinal rainy-day sin of fabric sweeping across a wet sidewalk.

And while metallic heeled sandals certainly aren’t the first shoes I’d recommend for trekking across Manhattan in a storm, I appreciate a Queen who commits. Fashion Week does occasionally require accepting that practicality has its limits.

The styling trick: A hood or headscarf can function as both rain protection and an accessory, especially when the rest of the outfit is doing something fun.

DashDividers_1_500x100

This is exactly the kind of high-low styling I want to see during Fashion Week. A sporty, oversized track jacket is inherently practical for unpredictable weather (even if it is Saint Laurent), but pairing it with black capri leggings makes the whole thing feel intentional rather than purely functional.

The woven black shoulder bag adds another texture element without competing with the jacket, while the cropped leggings solve the wet-hem problem entirely. It’s also proof that you don’t necessarily need a classic trench to dress for drizzle. A lightweight technical layer can be just as useful (and, in my humble opinion, considerably more interesting).

The styling trick: Let your outerwear handle the weather, then use an unexpected texture underneath to make the outfit feel styled.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Rainy weather has a way of convincing you that the only reasonable outfit involves pants. This look makes a strong argument for ignoring that instinct.

A distressed brown leather bomber gives a colorful button-down and red plaid mini skirt just enough protection without hiding the entire look beneath a traditional raincoat. The chunky clogs are also a smart move: the substantial sole creates some distance between your feet and the sidewalk while playing into the slightly undone, downtown feel of the look.

What really works is the balance. The skirt and bright layers feel playful, while the leather jacket and grounded footwear keep everything from veering into school-uniform territory.

The styling trick: If you’re wearing a mini in the rain, counterbalance the exposed leg with a substantial jacket and sturdy shoe.

I unintentionally put one of my favorite rainy-day rules to the test during NYFW: when puddles are inevitable, keep your hem off the ground. I paired black pleated culottes with a fluid funnel-neck blouse and brown heeled loafers, which gave me all the polish of a trouser-and-heel combination without having to worry about several inches of soaked fabric dragging behind me.

Accessories did most of the heavy lifting here. A slim black belt gave the loose silhouettes some definition, while a long tassel necklace, pearl earrings, and a silk scarf kept all those office-inspired separates from feeling too corporate. And yes, I carried a black umbrella. With an outfit this neutral, anything brighter would have felt like an uninvited plus-one.

The styling trick: When rain is in the forecast, trade floor-skimming trousers for a cropped wide-leg silhouette and stick with a substantial closed-toe shoe.

title: e.l.f.’s New Lip & Cheek Stain Is Sheer, Long-Lasting, & Only $6
text:
e.l.f.’s New Lip & Cheek Stain Is Sheer, Long-Lasting, & Only $6

Our team tests thousands of beauty products, at every price point, 365 days a year, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Many are fine, some are good — and then there are the ones that are great. My latest impressive beauty discovery comes in the form of e.l.f. Cosmetics’ new Sheer For It Blush Tints, and you’re about to see why.

Available in nine shades and priced at just $6 each — meaning you could theoretically buy the entire lineup for less than the price of a single luxury blush — Sheer For It is a lightweight, buildable cheek tint designed to deliver anything from a barely-there wash of color to a more saturated flush. The range spans soft pinks, berry tones, warm browns, and vibrant reds, with a sheer finish that can be layered to your desired level of intensity. It’s the kind of low-commitment, high-payoff blush that makes a strong case for keeping one in every makeup bag. (Sounds too good to be true, but then again, it’s what we’ve come to expect from the editor-beloved brand.) 

Ahead, three Refinery29 editors put e.l.f.’s Sheer For It Blush Tints to the test to see whether this $6 cheek tint is actually worth the hype. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: So Petal, Cherry Cola

“I’ve tried countless lip and cheek tints in my day, so when I tell you I audibly gasped when I swiped on e.l.f.’s Sheer For It, that’s saying something. This feels like a true, watery stain, but packs an impressive amount of pigment. One layer dotted onto cheeks and swiped on lips lends a kiss of color, but after I let that dry, I was able to layer this stuff on really well; two coats left a visible pop of color, and three rendered it as bold as a powder formula. But because it’s so lightweight, three layers still felt like I was wearing nothing. I will say, these set pretty quickly, so my preferred way to apply them was to dot and blend right away since you do not have a lot of play time. I don’t typically love pink shades on me, but So Petal (a cool, mid-tone pink) was surprisingly flattering on my olive skin. Then there was Cherry Cola, a burnt reddish hue that is more of what I typically gravitate towards. As the name suggests, the color payoff mimics what your lips look like after eating a bowl of cherries – flushed but not in a makeup-y way. Both shades lasted all day (even through sweaty workouts and heat waves) and didn’t transfer or disappear after eating or drinking. Consider me seriously impressed.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Writer

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: Left On Red

“Confession: liquid tints scare me a little. I like to take my time when applying makeup. And some formulas dry far too quickly for me to blend them out evenly, leaving me with pinches of color rather than the plump, juicy, and defined cheeks I’m after. This, however, boasts just the right consistency, meaning it doesn’t lock onto skin as quickly as the others, so I can take my fluffy brush — or a finger, if I’m so inclined — and tap it into the rest of my makeup without panicking. Left On Red lends my light olive skin the perfect natural flush, like I’ve been outside in the cold and my cheeks have become wind-dappled. Rather than swipe, I apply a few dots over my cheeks and use a dense fluffy brush (with a little primer on the bristles first) to make the final result more uniform. I also dust a touch of translucent powder over the top to diffuse. And the staying power! It’s second to none. Other cheek tints either make a hole in my foundation base or disappear within a few hours, but this one clung on until I removed my makeup at the end of the day. I use it on my lips, too.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Beauty Director

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: Mauve Actually

“At first glance, this liquid blush looked genuinely intimidating. Between its ultra-fluid, watery consistency and deep Onyx hue, I was terrified it was going to splash everywhere and ruin my white top the second I pulled out the applicator. Thankfully, the wand holds onto the formula well, no messy drips in sight.

Because of how rich the pigment looked in the bottle, I started cautiously with two tiny dabs on each cheek. Once blended, however, it seemed to completely disappear into my deep skin tone. Realizing just how sheer and buildable the formula is, I decided to be much more generous. Layer after layer (I ended up doing about four rounds), my skin seemed to absorb it almost like a hydrating moisturizer. As I continued building the color, a soft, subtle rosiness began to show through. Despite how deep the shade appears in the bottle, the formula applies much sheerer than I expected, which gave me plenty of control over the intensity. I preferred building it up for a more noticeable flush, but the lightweight texture made layering easy without feeling heavy on my skin.

Don’t let the dark initial shade intimidate you: for deeper complexions, a heavy hand and multiple layers are key to getting the color payoff to pop. To finish the look, I tapped a bit onto my lips over a brown lip liner, and it created the most flattering, natural rosy flush. If you’re looking for a versatile, multi-use flush of color that’s easy to layer into your routine, grab it—you won’t regret it.”—Alexis Bennett Parker, Shopping Director

title: How Rizos Curls’ Julissa Prado Gets It All Done as a Multi-Hyphenate Latina
text:
How Rizos Curls’ Julissa Prado Gets It All Done as a Multi-Hyphenate Latina

Sponsor Disclaimer: This article and accompanying podcast episode were sponsored by TextNow.

There’s no shortage of rules for how a Latina is supposed to live. Be ambitious, pero no te pases. Make your family proud, but don’t take up too much space. Work hard, but don’t make anyone uncomfortable by wanting more. And if you dare to question any of it? Well, you might just be called “una sinvergüenza.” Sound familiar?

For too long, that word has been used as a shaming tactic to silence us and put us in our so-called place. But what if we reclaim it? To me, being a sinvergüenza is being a woman without shame — living fully, taking up space, speaking our truth, and reclaiming the parts of ourselves we’ve been told to hide. And aren’t we deserving of that? I think so.

That’s why Somos launched Sin Vergüenza, a biweekly podcast for young Latinas who are figuring out how to live their best, most authentic lives, even when the world around us feels anything but easy. Each episode tackles the questions and challenges that come with being a multidimensional Latina today, from mental health, colorism, and dating to career negotiations, buying your first home, and everything in between. We’re bringing in Latina experts who get it to offer the insight, honesty, and guidance we don’t always have access to.

And we’re kicking things off with a conversation we know many of you will resonate with: How the hell are we supposed to get everything done?

According to a 2026 study from the Latino Donor Collaborative and Kantar, 61% of Latinas have multiple streams of income. Whether it’s because of economic uncertainty or a changing work culture, more of us are juggling multiple jobs, side projects, and personal brands. And not all of us are pulling it off. At least, not without burning ourselves out. For some, it’s the pressure to end generational poverty for ourselves and our loved ones. For others, it’s about making room for all the professional and creative parts of ourselves that we refuse to fit into a single box.

Whatever the reason, the work — and the to-do list — keeps piling up. So how do we actually do it all without completely running ourselves into the ground? Enter Julissa Prado. As the founder of Rizos Curls, the self-funded, multimillion-dollar haircare brand rooted in culture and community, Prado knows what it means to build something meaningful while balancing all the other pieces of her life. In our first episode of Sin Vergüenza, she gets real about how she manages it all and why doing more doesn’t necessarily mean doing everything at once.

Prado shares the strategies, patience, boundaries, and yes, self-love that have helped her grow Rizos Curls while making space for herself along the way. From a grading system that helps her prioritize the items on her to-do list to only putting on her plate what she’d serve her own figurative daughter, she offers advice for anyone trying to build a career, pursue a dream, care for the people they love, and still have something left for themselves at the end of the day.

Welcome to Sin Vergüenza, where young Latinas come to figure life out without shame, judgment, or the pressure to have it all together.

title: The Silence At The 2026 Emmys Spoke Volumes — Whiter, Quieter & Way Too Comfortable
text:
The Silence At The 2026 Emmys Spoke Volumes — Whiter, Quieter & Way Too Comfortable

For the first time in five years, no actor of color won a major acting Emmy during the primetime broadcast. It’s an awkward fact to sit with after a night of speeches about the importance of storytelling, artistic communities, and television’s allegedly limitless capacity to reflect the world back at us. The winners were talented, but that’s not the point. For an industry that has spent years promising audiences it is finally serious about representation, the 2026 Emmys delivered a familiar image: a parade of white acting winners accepting trophies while actors of color watched from their tables.

And yes, I understand the Emmys are an awards show. It’s built around expensive gowns, nervous clapping and television stars pretending they didn’t rehearse their acceptance speeches in the mirror. But awards matter. No matter how much glitter you throw at it, art will always be political. The same goes for the award shows celebrating it. They shape whose work gets remembered, whose career gets a jetpack and what kinds of stories studios decide are worth funding next time around.

This year’s result followed the least diverse Emmy nominations slate in a decade. By the end of the main telecast, the major acting honours had gone to Noah Wyle, Rhea Seehorn, Jean Smart, Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn and Stephen Root. One thing they all had in common was that they were white. It was a rough outcome for a field that included performers such as Sterling K. Brown, Zendaya, Quinta Brunson, Ayo Edebiri, Janelle James, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Chase Infiniti.

The night was not entirely without politics, but it just felt oddly restrained considering the conditions surrounding it. Sally Field won the Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for Remarkably Bright Creatures and gave the sort of speech that made the room feel briefly connected to the actual world. The series was shot in Canada, which prompted Field to call the country “Blessed Canada! Our neighbours, our friends”. In another year, that might have simply been a location shout-out. Given the Trump administration’s trade dispute with Canada, it landed with rather more force (although still dancing on the line of palatable politics). Field continued, saying: “We’re the arts. We matter. Our voices matter. Our diversity, our unique storytelling, matters. We can’t let those voices be silenced or compromized or merged.”

The final word was doing some heavy lifting there, pointing to Paramount Skydance’s proposed $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which continues to hang over Hollywood. David Ellison runs Paramount Skydance, but the deal is backed in part by his father, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who seems to be in a bromance with Donald Trump. The family’s links to the US president have attracted scrutiny, particularly because Trump has publicly said he would like CNN, currently owned by Warner Bros. Discovery, to end up in Paramount’s hands.

The deal is currently stalled by an antitrust challenge brought by a group of state attorneys general, led by California. If it proceeds, it would put major studios, streamers, cable brands, and news outlets under one corporate roof, meaning fewer companies and people would have a huge say over what gets made, who gets hired, and which stories reach an audience. That could have devastating consequences.

That backdrop made Stephen Colbert’s win for The Late Show feel a little heavier than the usual awards-show victory lap. CBS cancelled the program earlier this year, calling it “purely a financial decision”, and its final episode aired in May. Trump had made no secret of his contempt for Colbert or the show. When CBS announced the cancellation, he wrote on Truth Social that he “absolutely love[d] that Colbert got fired”, and later celebrated the final episode by calling Colbert “a total jerk”.

Colbert did not turn his Emmy acceptance speech into a long grievance session; instead, he spoke about the people whose jobs disappeared with the show. “The thing about these late shows is that, besides bringing a really good, steady job, is that they require so many people that they’re a fantastic incubator for young people to come in to learn to work professionally on a deadline in cooperation, in collaboration, and that is the future of our business that we have to look after,” he said.

That was the closest the Emmys got to reckoning with the people left exposed by an entertainment industry that keeps demanding fewer workers do more work, for less certainty, while executive suites pursue bigger deals. The Television Academy itself had already made that tension impossible to ignore. Before the ceremony, it moved five categories out of the primetime broadcast: supporting actor and actress in a limited or anthology series or movie, directing and writing for limited or anthology series or movies, and writing for a variety series. The Academy said it wanted “a fresh new take on the Emmys broadcast,” but SAG-AFTRA, the WGA, and the DGA criticized the move.

“The decision to eliminate these categories from the prime-time broadcast devalues the contributions of the talented people the Academy is meant to honour,” the guilds said in a joint statement. “An awards show dedicated to recognising excellence should not reduce recognition for the artists whose work gives it meaning.”

It’s hard to argue with that. Last year, the Emmys had a much more visible political current. Hannah Einbinder used her win to say “Fuck ICE” and call for a “Free Palestine”. Javier Bardem wore a keffiyeh and spoke against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and several attendees wore Artists4Ceasefire pins. Television Academy chair Cris Abrego also used the stage to criticize Congress for voting to defund the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Tramell Tillman made history as the first Black actor to win Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series.

This year Jean Smart made history by becoming the first woman to win an acting Emmy for every single season of a show’s run. However, this year there was also no comparable collective show of dissent from the stage or the red carpet, despite the genocide in Gaza continuing, the US media landscape becoming even more politically charged, and a major corporate takeover fight playing out in Hollywood’s backyard.

If I wanted to be generous, I’d say that absence doesn’t mean every winner owed viewers a geopolitical statement. People can accept an Emmy without becoming a full-time spokesperson for every injustice on Earth. But when the entertainment industry speaks so often about courage, community and the power of art, its biggest night can feel strangely hollow when so few people are willing to connect those ideas to the present tense.

Sally Field did. Alan Cumming did too, using his acceptance speech to say: “The time for talk is over. It is now time to vote, America.” There were flickers of urgency. Mostly though, the 2026 Emmys played it safe… and very white. And perhaps that is the clearest political statement of all.

From PEDESTRIAN.TV
